title: Plantar Fasciitis
overview: Plantar fasciitis is pain at the site where the plantar fascia attaches to the calcaneus (heel bone), sometimes called calcaneal enthesopathy, with or without pain along the medial band of the fascia. It is the most common cause of heel pain.
pathophysiology: Despite its name, plantar fasciitis usually shows no true inflammation; 'plantar fasciosis' is the more accurate term, reflecting a degenerative process from repetitive microtrauma rather than an inflammatory one. The plantar fascia is a band of tissue connecting the heel bone to the base of the toes, and repeated strain leads to micro-tearing and degeneration at its origin.
symptoms: Heel pain that is worse with the first steps in the morning or after periods of rest
Pain that often improves somewhat with continued activity, then worsens again later in the day
Pain along the medial (inner) band of the plantar fascia in some cases
causes: Tightness or contracture of the Achilles tendon and plantar fascia
Repetitive strain from prolonged standing, walking, or running on hard surfaces
risk_factors: Sedentary lifestyle or occupation requiring prolonged standing
Very high or very low (flat) arches
Associated conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or reactive arthritis (bilateral symptoms should raise suspicion of an inflammatory cause)
diagnosis: Diagnosis is mainly clinical, based on history and physical examination; imaging is occasionally used to rule out other causes of heel pain.
differential_diagnosis: Inferior calcaneal bursitis (sharper, more acute pain)
S1 radiculopathy from an L5 disk herniation (pain radiating from the low back to the heel)
treatment: Activity modification: shorter steps, avoiding barefoot walking and high-impact activities such as jogging
Achilles tendon and plantar fascia stretching exercises
In-shoe heel cushioning and arch-supporting orthotics
Night splints that keep the Achilles tendon and fascia stretched during sleep
Physical therapy, started early, to build a consistent daily stretching routine
Occasionally, glucocorticoid injections for persistent pain
when_to_see_a_doctor: If heel pain persists despite stretching, footwear changes, and rest, or if the pain is present in both feet (which may suggest an underlying inflammatory condition).

title: Bunion (Hallux Valgus)
overview: A bunion is a prominence of the medial portion of the head of the first metatarsal bone, associated with a lateral deviation of the big toe (hallux valgus).
pathophysiology: The cause is often a combination of genetic predisposition and biomechanical factors affecting the position of the first metatarsal bone or big toe. Laxity at the first tarsometatarsal joint allows the metatarsal to rotate in the frontal plane, causing the hallux to deform in the transverse plane and angulate laterally. Joint misalignment leads to secondary osteoarthritis with cartilage erosion and bone spur (exostosis) formation, which can progressively limit joint motion (hallux limitus) or eliminate it entirely (hallux rigidus). An adventitious bursa can develop medial to the joint prominence and become painful, swollen, and inflamed.
symptoms: Pain at the joint prominence, initially triggered by certain shoes
Tenderness of the joint capsule at any stage
Painful, warm, reddened, fluctuant swelling located medially (adventitious bursitis) in later stages
Swelling and mild inflammation affecting the whole joint
Restricted passive joint motion, dorsolateral tenderness, and increased dorsiflexion of the distal phalanx in hallux limitus/rigidus
causes: Genetic predisposition
Excessive foot pronation
Wearing tight, narrow, or pointed-toe shoes
Trauma (occasionally)
risk_factors: Frequent use of narrow or high-heeled shoes
diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and usually straightforward on physical examination; the lateral sesamoid may be visible in the intermetatarsal space on imaging, and in severe deformity the hallux may overlap or underlap the second toe.
differential_diagnosis: Osteoarthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint
treatment: Shoes with a wide toe box
Protective pads and orthotics
Glucocorticoid injection for bursitis or synovitis
Oral NSAIDs for joint pain
For hallux limitus/rigidus: orthotics or shoes that reduce motion or stress at the joint
Surgical intervention (e.g., osteotomy, arthrodesis) for refractory pain or difficulty walking
when_to_see_a_doctor: If pain, swelling, or joint stiffness interferes with walking or persists despite shoe changes and orthotics.

title: Achilles Tendinopathy
overview: Achilles tendinopathy is a painful condition of the Achilles tendon, the tough band of tissue connecting the calf muscles to the heel bone. It is very common among runners.
pathophysiology: During running, the calf muscles assist the lift-off phase of gait. Repetitive forces from running, combined with insufficient recovery time, can injure the Achilles tendon. Use of fluoroquinolone antibiotics increases the risk of tendinopathy and tendon rupture, particularly in people over age 60.
symptoms: Pain in the lower calf and back of the heel, usually the first symptom
Pain that increases when exercise begins and often lessens as exercise continues
Pain that worsens with continued activity over time
causes: Repetitive strain from running or similar high-impact activity
Insufficient recovery time between training sessions
risk_factors: Use of fluoroquinolone antibiotics, especially in people over 60
Tight calf muscles or limited ankle flexibility
diagnosis: Usually based on symptoms and physical examination; imaging (ultrasound or MRI) is sometimes needed to confirm the diagnosis or assess severity.
treatment: Ice and NSAIDs to relieve pain and inflammation
Avoiding running and cycling while pain persists
Stretching and strengthening exercises for the calf muscles, started as soon as they can be performed without pain
Resistance (eccentric) exercise to help prevent future injury
Shoes with flexible soles or heel lifts to reduce tension on the tendon
when_to_see_a_doctor: If heel and calf pain persists despite rest and stretching, or worsens progressively, especially in people over 60 taking fluoroquinolone antibiotics.

title: Hammer Toe Deformity
overview: Hammer toe deformity results from an imbalance of the digital extensor and flexor tendons, typically causing a contracture at the proximal interphalangeal joint of a toe (usually the second).
pathophysiology: The tendon imbalance leads to misalignment of the joint surfaces. As the deformity becomes more rigid, the altered function of the toe creates a retrograde buckling force at the metatarsal head, causing excessive plantar pressure during walking. This progresses to a fixed, Z-shaped deformity that can lead to dorsal subluxation and eventual dislocation at the metatarsophalangeal joint.
symptoms: Pain while wearing shoes, especially those with low or narrow toe boxes
Sometimes accompanying metatarsalgia (pain in the ball of the foot)
Visible fixed Z-shaped bend of the toe
causes: Tendon imbalance leading to joint surface misalignment
Often associated with bunions or other forefoot deformities
diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical; weight-bearing radiographs help determine the severity of the deformity. Joints should be examined for coexistent arthritis.
treatment: Shoes with a wide toe box
Taping or splinting the toe in plantarflexion to temporarily reduce the deformity
Toe pads and orthotics
Surgical correction considered for refractory symptoms
when_to_see_a_doctor: If toe pain persists despite footwear changes, or if the deformity becomes rigid and interferes with walking.

title: Medial and Lateral Plantar Nerve Entrapment
overview: Medial and lateral plantar nerve entrapment is compression of a branch of the posterior tibial nerve at the inner part of the heel and the proximal arch of the foot.
pathophysiology: Nerve branches become pinched between bone, ligaments, and connective tissue. Ankle movement and certain shoes or activities increase pressure on the already-compressed nerve, sustaining the pain.
symptoms: Near-constant pain, present while walking as well as sitting
Difficulty simply standing
Chronic pain that is worsened by high-impact activity such as running
Usually no burning, numbness, or tingling (unlike other nerve entrapments)
causes: Mechanical entrapment of the nerve between bone, ligaments, and connective tissue
Repetitive ankle movement
Footwear or activities that increase pressure on the nerve
risk_factors: Poorly fitted or overly tight footwear
diagnosis: Diagnosis is mainly clinical, based on history and foot examination.
differential_diagnosis: Tarsal tunnel syndrome (in which Tinel's sign is present, unlike in plantar nerve entrapment)
diagnostic_signs: Absence of other tarsal tunnel syndrome signs (e.g., Tinel's sign)
Symptoms reproducible by palpation proximal to the abductor hallucis and/or the plantar fascia origin at the medial calcaneal tuberosity
Medial nerve entrapment: pain in the proximal medial arch
treatment: Splints and orthotics to limit pressure on the nerve
Physical therapy
Footwear and activity modification
Immobilization in some cases
when_to_see_a_doctor: If pain while walking or sitting persists and does not improve with rest and footwear changes.

title: Freiberg Disease
overview: Freiberg disease is avascular necrosis of a metatarsal head, most often the second, resulting in progressive flattening of the metatarsal head.
pathophysiology: The disease is caused by repetitive microtrauma to the metaphysis and growth plate. The resulting avascular necrosis progressively flattens the metatarsal head, and the metatarsal joint tends to collapse over time.
symptoms: Weight-bearing forefoot pain at the affected metatarsal head
Pain particularly noticeable during push-off or when wearing high-heeled shoes
Possible swelling of the metatarsophalangeal joint
Painful limitation of passive joint motion
causes: Repetitive microtrauma to the metatarsal metaphysis and growth plate
Predisposing bone structure: a short first metatarsal or long second metatarsal, increasing stress on the second metatarsal head
risk_factors: Adolescence in girls, during rapid growth (puberty)
Dancing, jogging, and running, which repetitively stress the metatarsal joint and accelerate the process
diagnosis: Confirmed by radiographs; MRI may also be used to confirm the diagnosis.
treatment: Shoe changes or orthotics as first-line treatment
Immobilization in some cases
Surgical excision of the metatarsal head considered for advanced or refractory cases
when_to_see_a_doctor: If forefoot pain persists in a growing adolescent, particularly if worsened by heeled shoes or intense sports activity.

title: Plantar Fibromatosis
overview: Plantar fibromatosis is a benign (non-cancerous) proliferation of the connective tissue of the plantar fascia, presenting as fibrous nodules along the sole of the foot.
pathophysiology: Fibrous nodules develop along the plantar fascia and are most easily seen when the foot is dorsiflexed against the leg. It is a benign proliferative process without a single clearly established causal mechanism.
symptoms: Firm nodules under the sole of the foot, most visible when the foot is flexed upward
Pain or swelling of the foot
Sometimes inability to fully straighten the toes
Similar nodules often present in the palm of the hand (Dupuytren contracture)
causes: Benign proliferation of the plantar fascia's connective tissue; the precise mechanism is not fully understood
risk_factors: Reported, though possibly anecdotal, associations with diabetes, epilepsy, and alcohol use disorder
diagnosis: Diagnosis is based on clinical examination of the foot.
treatment: No treatment needed if nodules are asymptomatic
Orthotics to redirect pressure away from the nodular lesions when weight-bearing pain occurs
Glucocorticoid injections directly into the nodule if needed
complications: Surgical excision usually leads to recurrence, and sometimes to painful scar tissue requiring further surgery
Excessive removal of the fascia can cause unintended foot instability
when_to_see_a_doctor: If the nodules become painful with weight-bearing or interfere with walking or toe extension.

title: Tibialis Posterior Tendinosis and Tenosynovitis
overview: The tibialis posterior tendon helps maintain the normal arch of the foot. Its tendinosis is a chronic degenerative condition that can thicken the tendon and compromise muscle strength; tenosynovitis is inflammation of the synovial sheath surrounding the same tendon. Together, they are the most common causes of pain behind the medial malleolus.
pathophysiology: Tendon degeneration results from long-standing biomechanical problems (excessive pronation, often in people who are obese; hindfoot valgus; chronic tenosynovitis). A tarsal coalition of the hindfoot can create a rigid flatfoot deformity and limit tendon function. Tenosynovitis begins with acute inflammation of the tendon sheath, sometimes linked to primary inflammatory diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, gout).
symptoms: Occasional pain behind the inner ankle at first, triggered by activity
Pain that worsens over time, accompanied by swelling in the area
Progressive difficulty standing normally, walking, and rising on the toes
Inability to rise on the toes if the tendon is fully torn
Sudden flattening of the arch (arch collapse) if the tendon ruptures, with pain that can extend to the sole
causes: Excessive ongoing tension related to foot biomechanics (excessive pronation)
Pre-existing low arch
Hindfoot valgus
Chronic tenosynovitis
Tendon rupture in older adults or those with pre-existing chronic dysfunction
risk_factors: A foot that turns outward when walking
diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical; palpating the tendon during plantarflexion and inversion against resistance is usually painful.
differential_diagnosis: Other causes of medial ankle pain and arch collapse
treatment: Orthotics to support the arch
Immobilization depending on severity
Anti-inflammatory treatment
Surgery for rupture or advanced disease
complications: Without rupture, the height of the medial arch gradually decreases in chronic forms
May progress to degenerative changes of the subtalar joint and eventual arthritis
when_to_see_a_doctor: As soon as persistent pain develops behind the inner ankle, before it worsens or leads to arch collapse.

title: Metatarsophalangeal Joint Pain
overview: Pain in the joints of the forefoot (metatarsophalangeal joints) can arise from the joints themselves and is a common cause of metatarsalgia.
pathophysiology: Pain frequently results from misalignment of the joint surfaces with altered foot biomechanics, causing joint subluxation, plantar plate tears, capsular impingement, and cartilage destruction (osteoarthritis). The second metatarsophalangeal joint is often affected, developing collateral ligament laxity from tendon imbalance and hammer toe deformities. Functional hallux limitus (restricted motion of the first joint) can also be a cause, progressively leading to hallux rigidus with loss of joint mobility.
symptoms: Pain and swelling of the affected joint
Pain with walking
Pain on dorsal and plantar palpation and with passive motion
Mild swelling with minimal warmth possible in osteoarthritis
Significant warmth, swelling, or redness suggesting inflammatory arthropathy or infection
causes: Misalignment of the joint surfaces compressing the joint lining
Rheumatoid arthritis or psoriatic arthritis causing joint inflammation
Hammer toes worsening pain and misalignment
Natural thinning of the protective fat pad under the forefoot with age
Functional hallux limitus progressing to hallux rigidus
diagnosis: Based mainly on history and physical examination; infection or arthropathy should be excluded when inflammatory signs are present.
differential_diagnosis: Interdigital (Morton's) neuroma, usually differentiated by the absence of burning, numbness, and interdigital tingling
Infection or inflammatory arthropathy when significant warmth/redness/swelling are present
treatment: Appropriate orthotics
Shoes with good cushioning and adequate forefoot room
when_to_see_a_doctor: If forefoot pain persists or is accompanied by visible swelling, warmth, or redness.

title: Achilles Tendon Bursitis
overview: Achilles tendon bursitis is inflammation of a fluid-filled sac (bursa) at the heel. It is classified as posterior (between the skin and the Achilles tendon) or anterior/retrocalcaneal (in front of the tendon's insertion onto the calcaneus).
pathophysiology: Posterior bursitis occurs in response to pressure from a shoe on a bursa that forms at the top edge of the heel counter, between the skin and the Achilles tendon. Anterior (retrocalcaneal) bursitis affects a deeper bursa in front of the tendon; swelling initially localizes just in front of the tendon and gradually extends medially and laterally.
symptoms: Swelling, warmth, pain, and tenderness behind the heel
A small tender, erythematous or skin-colored nodule (posterior bursitis)
Pain on medial and lateral palpation of the tendon with the ankle in maximal dorsiflexion (anterior bursitis)
Pain when rising on the toes
causes: Repetitive pressure on the soft tissue at the back of the heel from a rigid shoe heel counter
Shoes that narrow toward the back of the heel (high heels, pumps)
A bony prominence of the calcaneus (Haglund deformity) contributing to posterior bursitis
risk_factors: Occurs mainly in young women, but can also affect men
diagnosis: Based on symptoms and clinical examination, sometimes supplemented with imaging (radiographs).
differential_diagnosis: Fracture of the posterolateral talar tubercle (pain in front of the tendon insertion)
Achilles tendon enthesopathy (pain mainly at the tendon insertion, without soft-tissue lesion)
Achilles tendon xanthoma (a pink, usually asymptomatic nodule, rare)
treatment: Shoe modification (low heels, well-fitted)
Anti-inflammatory treatment
Local glucocorticoid injection possible for anterior bursitis
Relief of pressure at the back of the heel
when_to_see_a_doctor: If pain, swelling, or warmth behind the heel persists despite shoe changes.

title: Pain in the Ball of the Foot (Metatarsalgia)
overview: Metatarsalgia is a general term for pain in the area of the metatarsophalangeal joints. It is not a single disease but a symptom that can have many different causes.
pathophysiology: Developing one condition that causes forefoot pain often contributes to the development of another condition causing pain in the same area, creating an intertwined cycle of biomechanical, inflammatory, nerve-related, or degenerative causes.
symptoms: Pain localized under the forefoot, with walking or weight-bearing
causes: Arthritis of the forefoot joints
Nerve compression between the toes (interdigital/Morton's neuroma)
Postural foot problems (excessive pronation, hallux limitus)
Sesamoiditis
Freiberg disease
Metatarsophalangeal joint pain (subluxation, osteoarthritis)
risk_factors: Advanced age (thinning of the plantar fat pad)
diagnosis: Based on clinical examination of the foot, with systematic search for the specific underlying cause among the many possible etiologies.
treatment: Entirely dependent on the identified cause
Orthotics and appropriate footwear as a general measure
Specific treatment of the underlying condition once identified
when_to_see_a_doctor: If forefoot pain persists or worsens, to identify its precise cause rather than treating it blindly.

title: Tarsal Tunnel Syndrome
overview: Tarsal tunnel syndrome (posterior tibial nerve neuralgia) is pain in the ankle, foot, and sometimes the toes, caused by compression or injury of the posterior tibial nerve within the tarsal tunnel, a fibrous canal near the ankle.
pathophysiology: The posterior tibial nerve runs from the back of the calf to the heel and sole through the tarsal tunnel, where it divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves. When tissues near the tunnel become inflamed, they swell and compress the nerve, causing pain.
symptoms: Painful burning or tingling with walking or when wearing certain shoes
Pain that can extend into the foot and toes
Symptoms frequently reported to worsen at night
Possible Tinel's sign (radiating pain when the nerve is tapped)
causes: Fractures
Ankle swelling from heart failure or kidney failure
Hypothyroidism (perineural mucin deposition)
Gout or osteoarthritis causing joint inflammation
Flexor tendon synovitis, fibrosis, synovial cysts
Poor foot posture with excessive internal ankle rotation
No identifiable cause in about 20% of cases
diagnosis: Clinical examination of the foot supplemented by nerve conduction studies.
differential_diagnosis: Plantar fasciitis (sometimes mistaken for tarsal tunnel syndrome)
Medial and lateral plantar nerve entrapment (in which Tinel's sign is absent)
treatment: Steroid injections
Orthotics
Surgery in some refractory cases
when_to_see_a_doctor: If persistent pain, burning, or tingling in the ankle and foot occurs, especially if it worsens at night.

title: Sesamoiditis
overview: Sesamoiditis is pain affecting the two small, crescent-shaped sesamoid bones located beneath the head of the first metatarsal, where it meets the big toe, with or without associated inflammation or fracture.
pathophysiology: The two sesamoid bones (the tibial sesamoid medially, the fibular sesamoid laterally) sit within the tendon of the flexor hallucis brevis and assist foot locomotion. Direct trauma or a change in sesamoid positioning due to structural changes in the foot (such as lateral deviation linked to hallux valgus) can make them painful.
symptoms: Pain under the base of the big toe (under the first metatarsal head)
Pain worsened by walking, especially barefoot
Pain worsened by thin-soled, soft-soled, or high-heeled shoes
Area sometimes warm, swollen, with redness that may extend medially
causes: Repetitive injury to the sesamoid bones
Fracture of a sesamoid bone
Inflammation of the bones or adjacent tissue
Displacement of the sesamoids linked to structural changes of the foot (notably hallux valgus)
risk_factors: Presence of hallux valgus (many patients with a bunion also have tibial sesamoiditis)
diagnosis: Clinical examination of the foot.
differential_diagnosis: Gout (can sometimes be clinically confused with sesamoiditis)
treatment: Orthotics
Offloading pads
Shoe changes
when_to_see_a_doctor: If pain under the big toe persists or is accompanied by swelling, warmth, or redness.

title: Sever Disease (Calcaneal Apophysitis)
overview: Sever disease (apophysitis of the calcaneus) is inflammation of the heel's growth cartilage, occurring in children around the time of puberty. It is a type of osteochondrosis, a growth-plate disorder that occurs when a child grows rapidly.
pathophysiology: During a growth spurt, bones, muscles, and tendons develop at different rates. The calf muscle and Achilles tendon can tighten and pull on the growth cartilage where they attach at the heel, injuring and swelling the cartilage. The heel bone becomes fully solid by about age 15, after which the risk resolves.
symptoms: Pain on the sides or top of the heel
Pain worsened by standing on tiptoe or running
Warmth and redness in some children
Limping or avoiding weight-bearing on the affected heel
causes: Rapid growth during which bones develop faster than muscles and tendons
Tension of the calf muscle and Achilles tendon on the heel's growth cartilage
risk_factors: Children in puberty (generally 9-14 years old) with intense sports activity
Shoes that do not raise the heel (track shoes, football cleats)
diagnosis: Based on symptoms; radiographs do not confirm the diagnosis but help rule out other causes of heel pain (bone cysts, stress fractures).
treatment: Stretching the calf muscles and Achilles tendon before and after sports activity (prevention and relief)
Heel cups, pads, night splints
Sometimes a cast in more pronounced cases
Ice and rest
prognosis: Self-limiting condition: symptoms resolve once heel growth is complete, generally by around age 15.
when_to_see_a_doctor: If a child complains of persistent heel pain, especially if limping or avoiding normal walking.

title: Inferior Calcaneal Bursitis
overview: Inferior calcaneal bursitis is inflammation of the bursa located under the heel bone (calcaneus), near the insertion of the plantar fascia.
pathophysiology: The bursa normally acts as a cushion and reduces friction in areas where skin, muscles, tendons, and ligaments rub against bone. Its inflammation under the calcaneus causes sharp, acute pain, distinct from the dull, chronic pain typical of plantar fasciitis.
symptoms: Throbbing heel pain, especially when walking barefoot on hard surfaces
Heel that is mildly warm and swollen
Sharp, shooting pain that is most pronounced when the heel first strikes the ground while walking or running
causes: Inflammation of the bursa beneath the calcaneus, near the plantar fascia insertion
risk_factors: Frequent barefoot walking on hard surfaces
diagnosis: Diagnosis is mainly clinical, confirmed if needed by MRI (which can also exclude a calcaneal stress fracture).
differential_diagnosis: Plantar fasciitis (dull, chronic pain, in contrast to the acute pain of bursitis)
Fat pad syndrome (more common in older patients, related to thinning of the heel fat pad)
treatment: Injection of an anesthetic and glucocorticoid mixture into the bursa
Soft-soled shoes with protective heel cushioning
when_to_see_a_doctor: If throbbing heel pain persists, especially when walking barefoot on hard surfaces.

title: Morton's Neuroma
overview: Morton's neuroma is a thickening of the tissue around a nerve between the toes, most often between the third and fourth toes. It causes pain in the ball of the foot and is more common in women than in men.
pathophysiology: A nerve running between the long bones of the forefoot becomes compressed and irritated, and the tissue around it thickens over time.
symptoms: Numbness or tingling between the third and fourth toes
Sharp, shooting or burning pain in the ball of the foot, sometimes spreading to the toes
Cramping in the toes
Pain that gets worse with tight shoes, high heels or pressure on the forefoot
Symptoms that slowly worsen over time
causes: The exact cause is unknown
Tight shoes and high heels that squeeze the forefoot
Foot shape or toe position problems such as flat feet, high arches, bunions or hammer toes
risk_factors: Regular wear of tight or high-heeled shoes
Forefoot deformities such as bunions or hammer toes
diagnosis: Diagnosis is mostly clinical: the examiner often squeezes the forefoot to reproduce the symptoms. X-ray can look for bone problems, and ultrasound or MRI can confirm the diagnosis. Nerve conduction testing cannot diagnose it but can help rule out other causes, and blood tests may look for inflammatory arthritis.
treatment: Padding or taping of the forefoot
Orthotic shoe inserts
Wider shoes with a roomy toe box and low heels
Anti-inflammatory medicines or injections, not for long-term use
Physical therapy
Surgery to remove the thickened tissue and the inflamed nerve when other treatments fail; numbness in the toes afterwards is permanent
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional for constant pain in the foot or toes, or for tingling in the area.

title: Fungal Nail Infection (Onychomycosis)
overview: Onychomycosis is a fungal infection of the nails. It is much more common in toenails than in fingernails and in older adults, and it often starts after a fungal infection of the skin of the foot such as athlete's foot.
pathophysiology: Fungi invade the nail and the skin under it, where they feed on dead tissue. The infection clears only as a new, uninfected nail grows out.
symptoms: Brittle or crumbling nails with ragged edges
Thickened nail, often dull or distorted in shape
White or yellow streaks or patches on the nail
Debris collecting under the nail
Nail lifting or loosening from the nail bed
causes: Fungi that feed on dead tissue in the nails and the outer layer of the skin
Prolonged moisture and tight shoes that limit airflow
Minor nail or skin injuries and existing nail deformities
Athlete's foot spreading to the nail
risk_factors: Poor circulation or nerve disease in the limbs
diagnosis: A clinician examines the nails, and the diagnosis is confirmed by looking at nail scrapings under a microscope. A culture can identify the fungus but its result can take 4 to 6 weeks.
differential_diagnosis: Bacterial or yeast infection around the nail (paronychia)
treatment: Over-the-counter creams and ointments generally do not clear a nail infection
Prescription antifungal tablets, usually taken for about two to three months for toenails, with blood tests to monitor the liver
Laser therapy is sometimes used but is less effective than medication
Removal of the nail in some cases
The nail clears only as healthy nail grows out, which can take up to a year, and the infection can come back
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional if the nail infection does not improve with treatment, or if the area becomes painful, red or drains pus.

source.name: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: Fungal nail infection

title: Ingrown Toenail
overview: An ingrown toenail happens when the edge of a toenail grows into the skin beside it, causing pain, redness and swelling. It most often affects the big toe.
pathophysiology: The nail edge pierces or presses into the surrounding skin, which becomes inflamed and can become infected.
symptoms: Pain along the edge of the nail
Redness of the skin beside the nail
Swelling around the nail
causes: Tight or ill-fitting shoes, the most common trigger
Cutting the nails too short or rounding the corners
Stubbing the toe or other injury to the nail
Naturally curved or thick nails, and foot deformities
Picking at the corners of the nail
diagnosis: A clinician examines the toe and asks about the symptoms. Imaging or other tests are usually not needed.
differential_diagnosis: Infection of the skin fold beside the nail (paronychia)
treatment: Soaking the foot in warm water several times a day
Gently massaging the inflamed skin
Placing a small piece of cotton or floss under the edge of the nail
Wearing sandals or roomy shoes while it heals
A clinician or podiatrist may remove part of the nail after numbing the toe, and may prescribe antibiotics if it is infected
Trim nails straight across and never try to cut out the ingrown part yourself
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional promptly if you have diabetes, nerve damage, poor foot circulation or signs of infection (increasing pain, redness, swelling, pus or fever), or if home care does not help.

title: Plantar Warts
overview: Plantar warts are rough skin growths on the soles of the feet caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV). They can be painful and make walking difficult.
pathophysiology: HPV infects the skin of the sole, and the pressure of walking pushes the growth inward, which is why it can be painful.
symptoms: A rough, raised, round or oval growth on the sole of the foot
Skin colour lighter or darker than the surrounding skin
Pain, especially when walking or standing
causes: Infection of the skin with the human papillomavirus (HPV)
Spread by contact with a wart on the body or on another person
Walking barefoot around pools and showers
risk_factors: Walking barefoot in communal wet areas
diagnosis: Warts are usually diagnosed by examining the skin. A skin biopsy may be done to rule out other growths, such as skin cancer.
treatment: Cushioning pads, socks and roomy shoes to ease the pain
A clinician may trim the thick skin
Do not try to cut the wart out yourself
Over-the-counter wart medicines, or prescription medicines, freezing (cryotherapy), electrocautery, laser or immunotherapy if it persists
Most warts clear on their own, often within about two years, but plantar warts are harder to cure and can come back
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional for signs of infection (spreading redness, pus, discharge or fever), bleeding that does not stop, pain, a wart that changes colour or appearance, or if you have diabetes or a weakened immune system.

title: Athlete's Foot (Tinea Pedis)
overview: Athlete's foot is a fungal infection of the feet, most often between the toes. The fungus grows in warm, damp conditions and spreads by direct contact or through shared items.
pathophysiology: A skin fungus colonises the outer layer of the skin of the foot, especially in moist spaces between the toes.
symptoms: Cracked, flaking or peeling skin between the toes or along the sides of the foot
Redness and itching
Burning or stinging
Blisters that may ooze or crust
Discoloured, thick or crumbly nails if the infection spreads to them
causes: A fungus that grows on warm, damp skin
Closed shoes, especially plastic-lined ones, and feet that stay wet or sweaty
Walking barefoot in showers and pools, and sharing shoes or socks
Minor skin or nail injuries
diagnosis: A clinician can often diagnose it by examining the skin. A simple office test for fungus (KOH examination), a skin culture or a skin biopsy may be used if needed.
treatment: Over-the-counter antifungal creams or powders
Continue the treatment for one to two weeks after the symptoms clear to reduce the chance of return
Wash and dry the feet well, especially between the toes, and wear clean cotton socks
Choose well-ventilated shoes and alternate pairs so they dry fully
If there is no improvement after two to four weeks, prescription antifungal tablets or creams, or antibiotics for a secondary bacterial infection
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional promptly if the foot becomes swollen and warm or shows red streaks, increasing pain, pus or fever, and if there is no improvement after two to four weeks of self-care.

title: Corn (Heloma)
overview: A corn is a small area of thickened, hard skin that forms on the top or side of a toe in response to repeated pressure or friction, most often from shoes that fit badly.
pathophysiology: Skin protects itself from repeated rubbing or pressure by thickening.
symptoms: Thick, hard skin on a toe, sometimes flaky or dry
Pain when the area is pressed or rubbed by a shoe
Occasionally bleeding
causes: Shoes that fit badly and press or rub on the toe
Repeated pressure or friction on the same spot
risk_factors: Diabetes or numb feet (higher risk of complications)
diagnosis: A clinician usually diagnoses a corn by examining the skin. Tests are rarely needed.
treatment: Wear shoes that fit better, with enough room for the toes
Protect the area with a doughnut-shaped pad while it heals
Reducing friction is often the only treatment needed
If an infection or an ulcer develops, a clinician may need to remove the affected tissue and prescribe antibiotics
when_to_see_a_doctor: People with diabetes or numb feet should check their feet carefully and report any problem promptly. Anyone should seek care if a corn does not improve, or if there is persistent pain, redness, warmth or drainage.

source.name: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: Corns and calluses

title: Callus
overview: A callus is an area of thickened skin that forms on the soles of the feet, or on the hands, as a protective response to repeated pressure or friction. On the foot it can also form over a bunion, where the bone rubs against the shoe.
pathophysiology: Skin protects itself from repeated rubbing or pressure by thickening.
symptoms: A thick, hard patch of skin that may be dry or flaky
Pain, and sometimes bleeding
causes: Repeated pressure or friction on the skin
Foot conditions such as bunions or hammer toes that concentrate pressure on one spot
risk_factors: Diabetes or numb feet (higher risk of complications)
diagnosis: A clinician usually diagnoses a callus by examining the skin. Tests are rarely needed.
treatment: Reduce friction and pressure on the area
Treat the underlying problem, such as a bunion or hammer toe, so that the callus does not return
Wear well-fitting shoes
If an infection or an ulcer develops, a clinician may need to remove the affected tissue and prescribe antibiotics
when_to_see_a_doctor: People with diabetes or numb feet should check their feet carefully and report any problem promptly. Anyone should seek care if a callus does not improve, or if there is persistent pain, redness, warmth or drainage.

source.name: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: Corns and calluses

title: Diabetic Foot Ulcer
overview: A diabetic foot ulcer is an open sore on the foot of a person with diabetes. Because diabetes can damage nerves and blood vessels, the sore is often painless and heals poorly.
pathophysiology: Nerve damage reduces feeling, so injuries go unnoticed, while poor blood flow slows healing and pressure on one spot keeps the wound from closing.
symptoms: An open sore on the foot that is slow to heal
Often little or no pain because of reduced feeling
Signs of infection: redness, warmth or swelling around the wound, pus or odour, increased pain or firmness, fever or chills
Skin around the ulcer that looks very white, blue or black
causes: Nerve damage that reduces feeling, so injuries and blisters go unnoticed
Poor blood flow that slows healing
Too much pressure on one spot of the foot
risk_factors: Diabetes with poorly controlled blood sugar
diagnosis: A clinician examines the foot and the wound. Regular foot examinations are the best way to assess the risk of an ulcer.
treatment: Removal of dead tissue and cleaning of the wound by a clinician such as a podiatrist
Taking pressure off the ulcer with special shoes, a brace or cast, or crutches
Daily cleaning and bandaging with the dressings the clinician recommends
Keeping blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol under control, and stopping smoking
Do not remove dead tissue yourself, walk barefoot, or wear tight, open-toe or non-breathable shoes
when_to_see_a_doctor: Contact a healthcare professional promptly if there are signs of infection, or if the ulcer or the skin around it looks very white, blue or black, or if bone can be felt in the wound. Spreading redness, pus, fever or chills in a person with diabetes need urgent medical assessment.

source.name: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: Diabetes - foot ulcers

title: Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy of the Foot
overview: Diabetic neuropathy is nerve damage caused by diabetes. In the feet it first causes tingling, burning or pain, and later numbness.
pathophysiology: High blood sugar over many years and reduced blood flow injure the nerves, starting with the longest nerves that reach the toes and feet.
symptoms: Tingling, burning or deep pain that starts in the toes and feet
Loss of feeling that progresses over time until the skin is numb
Not noticing cuts, blisters, sharp objects or extreme heat or cold
Very dry, cracked skin on the feet
Excessive sweating of the feet early on
causes: High blood sugar over many years damaging the nerves
Reduced blood flow to the nerves
Poorly controlled diabetes; about half of people with diabetes develop it
diagnosis: A clinician checks reflexes and sensation (with a monofilament, vibration, temperature and joint position), looks at the skin and nails, and may order nerve conduction tests. Vitamin B12 level should also be checked.
differential_diagnosis: Other causes of peripheral neuropathy such as alcohol or kidney disease
treatment: Control blood sugar with healthy eating, regular exercise, monitoring and prescribed medicines
Medicines that relieve nerve pain
Daily foot care and regular foot examinations
Appropriate socks and shoes to prevent injuries from becoming serious
when_to_see_a_doctor: Contact a healthcare professional if any symptom of diabetic neuropathy develops. People with numb feet should check their feet every day for cuts and blisters.

source.name: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: Diabetes and nerve damage

title: Gout
overview: Gout is a form of arthritis caused by too much uric acid in the body. Uric acid crystals form in the joint fluid and trigger sudden attacks of pain, redness and swelling, most often in the big toe.
pathophysiology: Uric acid builds up because the body makes too much or removes too little, and crystals in the joint trigger inflammation.
symptoms: Sudden, severe joint pain, often starting at night
A red, warm, swollen and very tender joint
Most often the big toe, but also the knee or the ankle
A fever may occur
Attacks usually settle within days but often come back
causes: Uric acid building up because the body makes too much or removes too little
Alcohol, especially beer, red meat and sugary drinks
Kidney disease, obesity, diabetes and some medicines such as water pills
Family history
risk_factors: Male sex, or women after menopause
diagnosis: Doctors may analyse joint fluid for uric acid crystals and measure uric acid in the blood. A joint X-ray may look normal. A high blood uric acid does not always mean gout.
treatment: Treat an attack as soon as it begins with anti-inflammatory medicines, colchicine or corticosteroids
Pain often eases within 12 hours and is usually gone within 48 hours
Daily medicines that lower uric acid can prevent attacks
Less alcohol, weight loss, exercise, and limiting red meat and sugary drinks
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional for symptoms of an acute attack. A hot, red, swollen joint with fever needs prompt assessment, because a joint infection must be ruled out.

title: Hallux Rigidus (Stiff Big Toe)
overview: Hallux rigidus is arthritis of the main joint of the big toe. Worn cartilage and bone spurs make the toe painful and stiff. It is the most common arthritic condition of the foot and usually appears between the ages of 30 and 60.
pathophysiology: The cartilage that cushions the end of the bones wears down, bone spurs form on top of the joint and limit how far the toe can bend when walking.
symptoms: Pain in the big toe joint when walking or being active, usually on top of the joint
Stiffness and difficulty bending the toe up or down
Swelling around the joint, which may affect the choice of shoes
A bump on top of the foot near the big toe, sometimes red
causes: Gradual wear and tear of the joint cartilage
An earlier injury to the big toe
Poor foot alignment such as flat foot or bunions
Genetic factors
diagnosis: A clinician examines the joint, moves the toe to see how far it bends without pain, and checks for bone spurs. X-rays show the spurs and the loss of joint space. Early diagnosis makes treatment easier.
treatment: Pain relievers or anti-inflammatory medicines, by mouth or applied to the skin
Ice packs and alternating cold and warm water soaks
Shoes with a wide toe box, no high heels, and stiff or rocker-bottom soles
Corticosteroid injection into the joint
Surgery for advanced disease: removal of bone spurs (cheilectomy), joint fusion or joint replacement
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional if big toe pain or stiffness persists or limits walking, because treatment is easier before the arthritis is advanced.

source.name: AAOS OrthoInfo: Hallux Rigidus (Stiff Big Toe)

title: Ankle Sprain
overview: An ankle sprain is a stretch or tear of the ligaments that hold the ankle bones together. Sprains are graded from mild stretching (grade I) to a complete tear (grade III).
pathophysiology: A sudden twisting or rolling of the ankle overloads the ligaments on the outer side of the joint, which stretch or tear.
symptoms: Pain and swelling of the ankle
Bruising in more severe sprains, which can take up to about two weeks to fade
Difficulty walking
Sometimes long-term pain, swelling or weakness
causes: A sudden twisting or rolling injury of the ankle
risk_factors: Sports with jumping or sudden changes of direction
diagnosis: Diagnosis is made by examining the ankle. An X-ray is used when a fracture is suspected.
treatment: Rest and avoid putting weight on the foot at first
Raise the foot to or above heart level
Ice for about 20 minutes at a time, every hour while awake for the first 24 hours, then three to four times a day, with a cloth between the ice and the skin
Over-the-counter pain relievers, if safe for the person
A brace, splint or cast and crutches for more severe sprains; surgery is sometimes needed for a complete tear
Add weight gradually once pain and swelling settle, usually after about 48 hours; strengthening exercises help prevent another sprain
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional if walking is very painful or impossible, pain persists despite rest, ice and pain relievers, there is no improvement after 5 to 7 days, the ankle keeps giving way, or there is worsening discolouration, numbness, tingling or coldness.

source.name: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: Ankle sprain - aftercare

title: Metatarsal Stress Fracture
overview: A metatarsal stress fracture is a small crack in one of the long bones of the foot. It is caused by repeated strain over time rather than a single injury.
pathophysiology: Repeated loading of the bone is faster than its repair, so a small crack develops.
symptoms: Pain that appears during activity and eases with rest
Pain over a wide area of the foot at first, later constant and focused on one spot
Tenderness and swelling at the fracture site
causes: Repeated overuse of the foot in the same way
A sudden increase in activity
High-impact activities such as running, dancing, jumping or marching
risk_factors: Nerve damage in the feet, for example from diabetes
diagnosis: An X-ray may not show the fracture for up to six weeks, so a bone scan or MRI may be needed.
treatment: Rest, raise the foot and avoid the activity that caused the injury
Crutches if walking hurts and a clinician advises it
Over-the-counter pain relievers within the label limits, after checking with a clinician if there are other health problems
A supportive shoe, or a cast below the knee for severe pain
Healing usually takes four to twelve weeks; return to activity gradually, once it no longer hurts
when_to_see_a_doctor: Contact a healthcare professional if pain persists, gets worse, or is present at rest or at night. Seek prompt care if you cannot put weight on the foot or the foot looks deformed.

source.name: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: Metatarsal stress fractures - aftercare

title: Flat Feet (Pes Planus) in Adults
overview: Flat feet is a foot shape in which the arch does not form normally when standing. In adults, aging, injury or illness can damage the tendons that support the arch in a foot that used to have one, sometimes on one side only.
pathophysiology: Loose or weakened tendons and ligaments no longer support the joints of the foot. In adults a painful, progressively flattening arch is often due to failure of the posterior tibial tendon (see the posterior tibial tendinosis sheet).
symptoms: Many people have no symptoms
Tiredness or aching of the feet after long periods of standing or sport
Pain on the outer side of the ankle
In long-standing flat feet, changes in the shape and flexibility of the toes, which may become painful
causes: Loose tendons and ligaments that support the joints of the foot
Aging, injury or illness damaging the supporting tendons in adults
Inherited connective tissue conditions such as Ehlers-Danlos and Marfan syndromes
Rarely, two or more foot bones joined together (tarsal coalition)
diagnosis: A clinician checks whether an arch appears when standing on the toes: if it does, the flat foot is flexible and no further tests are usually needed. If no arch forms or there is pain, X-ray, CT or MRI can assess the bones, joints, tendons and ligaments.
treatment: Flexible flat feet that do not hurt need no treatment
If painful: store-bought or custom arch supports, supportive shoes and calf stretches
Rigid or painful flat feet need an evaluation by a clinician, because treatment depends on the cause
Pain relievers and orthotics in older adults
Surgery in severe cases: tendon repair or transfer, or fusion of foot joints in a corrected position
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional for persistent foot pain, or if a flat foot is rigid or painful.
